papers.title: Design and Evaluation of Epira: An Automated Interview System for Case Investigation and Contact Tracing
papers.abstract: Objective: Case investigation and contact tracing are labor-intensive. Web forms struggle when respondents need clarification before disclosing contacts, and open-ended chatbots may deviate from protocols. We developed and evaluated Epira, a protocol-controlled large language model (LLM) interviewer for multi-disease case investigation and contact tracing. Materials and Methods: Epira pairs LLM dialogue with a rule-based controller enforcing required questions, safety handoffs, and a structured case record, and adapts to new diseases by questionnaire upload. Local (Qwen2.5) and cloud (GPT-5.4) backends were tested. Study 1 used 108 simulated cases with ground-truth fields and contacts for measles and gonorrhea under Epira and open-ended conditions (864 sessions). Study 2 enrolled 72 volunteers in a 2$\times$2 disease-by-model interview assessing completion, usability, acceptability, and trust. Results: Across Study 1, Epira with a local LLM captured 88.9% of required fields and 60.1% of ground-truth contacts. Open-ended interviewers recovered 31.1-41.9 percentage points fewer required fields than the same models in Epira. In Study 2, completion was 100%; mean adapted System Usability Scale (SUS) was 82.95 $\pm$ 16.17 on a 0-100 scale and mean trust was 3.85 $\pm$ 0.77 on a 1-5 scale. Discussion: Protocol control drove completeness more than model choice. Local and cloud deployments produced similar records, supporting privacy-preserving local use with human review of routed interviews and missed contacts. Conclusion: Epira recovers required fields and contacts under diverse disclosure conditions, works with local and cloud LLMs, and received favorable usability and trust ratings.

papers.title: GenAI-DBT: Evaluating a DBT-Informed Generative AI Platform for Mindfulness Skills Training: A Pilot Randomized Study
papers.abstract: We evaluated the feasibility, acceptability, and engagement of three digital formats for dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) mindfulness skills training. In a 30-day randomized pilot study, 45 university students were assigned to GenAI-DBT, a general-purpose large language model chatbot (Chatbot), or a static web resource (Web). Forty-two completed the study, and nine completed follow-up interviews. Usability scores were within acceptable ranges across conditions, with no significant between-group differences. GenAI-DBT showed the highest observed participant-week adherence (71.4%, vs. 53.3% for Web and 42.3% for Chatbot), a descriptive difference. Mindful Attention Awareness Scale and Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale scores showed no significant time-by-group interactions, and session-level self-reported mood changes did not differ significantly across conditions. GenAI-DBT showed a larger positive change in linguistic valence than Chatbot (4.28 vs. 1.59, P = .02, Cohen's d = 0.99). Interviewees valued contextualized, scenario-based practice and identified response latency, repetition, and limited personalization as areas for improvement. The findings support the feasibility and acceptability of DBT-informed conversational AI for skills practice and motivate further evaluation in larger, more clinically relevant samples. Clinical efficacy remains to be established.

papers.title: A Foundation Model to Measure and Predict Human Behaviour
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to infer psychological attributes, predict individual behaviour, and simulate human populations. However, despite generating plausible responses, they often misrepresent individuals and distort population statistics. Here we introduce Chiron, a foundation model to measure and predict human behaviour. We jointly fine-tune an LLM to represent psychological constructs, predict individual behaviour, and align population response distributions with human statistics. The training and evaluation data span 36 behavioural domains and 78 social science experiments, comprising 288,307 person records, 1,411,750 atomic behavioural decisions, and 99,953 psychometric assessments over 109 psychological constructs. In our evaluations, Chiron's psychological measurements agree more closely with human self-reports and exhibit fewer biases that undermine psychometric validity. It predicts individual behaviour more accurately than frontier LLMs (up to 28.4% relative improvement). In simulations of social science experiments, it more accurately captures the direction and magnitude of human experimental effects (82.2--94.3% lower effect-size estimation error). Together, these results establish Chiron as a unified computational instrument for measuring and predicting human behaviour.

papers.title: AI as Anchor: How Interview Sequencing Relates to the Appropriation of Synthetic Stakeholder Voices in Design Education
papers.abstract: Designers increasingly use large language models to simulate stakeholder conversations. Yet it remains unclear how AI-Simulated Stakeholders (AIS) are taken up when used alongside human stakeholder engagement. We report a field study in a single-institution, single-semester design course in which 8 teams (N=21) constructed, evaluated, and peer-reviewed an initial AIS. Then, the teams interviewed both AIS and human stakeholders in two sequences: AIS-first or human-first. Drawing on interview transcripts, design artifacts, course-embedded reflections, and post-course qualitative sessions, we examine exploratory patterns associated with these sequencing conditions. We find that students did not describe AIS as a neutral addition to the process. Instead, the order in which AIS and human stakeholders were formally interviewed was associated with different ways of interpreting and using information from the two sources. When the AIS interview came first, it provided a broad but often general frame that students later reconsidered through human interviews. When the AIS interview followed human engagement, AIS was more often used to revisit and validate insights already grounded in lived experience. Students described AIS as an "anchor," but its reported role varied with its position in the formal interview sequence. In the final designs, a larger proportion of prominent human-stakeholder-derived concerns than AIS-derived concerns had corresponding design elements. We contribute: characterization of AIS as a reference point whose reported role varies with its position in the formal interview sequence; exploratory empirical evidence that the implemented interview-order conditions were associated with distinct patterns of interpreting and using stakeholder input; and implications for integrating AIS into design workflows in ways that preserve direct engagement with human stakeholders

papers.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

papers.title: Supporting Researcher Control in AI-Assisted Social Media Analysis: A Mixed-Methods Study of AI4OSN
papers.abstract: High-quality annotated datasets are critical for advancing computational social science (CSS) research, yet collecting, curating, and analyzing large-scale data from dynamic sources such as online social networks (OSNs) remains a persistent bottleneck. Researchers must also translate substantive questions into queries, relevance criteria, and defensible interpretations. Large language models (LLMs) can assist, but they can also obscure the judgments, potentially reducing researcher oversight and critical evaluation. We present AI4OSN, a mixed-initiative platform that keeps researchers in control of data collection, relevance labeling, and sensemaking while making AI assistance available as an inspectable advisory resource. In a systematic user study (N=18) using X/Twitter data, participants reported above-benchmark perceived usability (mean SUS score of 79.7), increased confidence in LLM-assisted annotation and analysis tasks, and low cognitive workload during AI-supported sensemaking. Notably, novice participants showed descriptively greater alignment and higher reported agreement with AI output than experienced participants, underscoring the need to support differentiated verification practices across expertise levels. Overall, this work contributes both a human-centered system for social data analysis and empirical insights into how AI-assisted interfaces shape researcher behavior, trust, and decision-making. Our findings highlight design opportunities and tensions in building accessible, transparent, and agentic AI systems for social media and web research.

papers.title: Edit Recommendation: Can LLMs Anticipate Edit Requests from Users, and When?
papers.abstract: After a large language model (LLM) agent generates an artifact, users often send edit requests for it. This paper studies whether an LLM can anticipate these requests before they are sent. Such anticipation is useful in practice because it reduces the effort of user review and feedback. We formalize this task as edit recommendation and build EditRecBench, a benchmark for evaluating the performance of LLMs on this task, from real-world conversation logs in WildChat-4.8M. Through benchmarking and failure analysis, we identify a practical challenge that some cases are inherently difficult to predict in real-world settings. To address this, we introduce decision model-based gating to filter out cases where predictions are unlikely to be correct before they are presented to the user. Our trained model outperforms existing decision models and raises pass@5 among shown suggestions by 12--25 points at a gating threshold. Our code is available at https://github.com/ntt-dkiku/llm-edit-recommendation.

papers.title: PromptPoseFX: Authoring Pose-Driven Visual Effects through Augmented Prompting and Interactive Refinement
papers.abstract: Human pose-driven visual effects offer a compelling way for enhancing video expressiveness and storytelling. Authoring such effects with traditional video editing tools is a complex and time-consuming task that requires considerable technical expertise and manual effort. While generative AI models can simplify the workflow by reducing manual scripting through language-driven generation, existing approaches suffer from imprecise alignment between visual effects and pose data, failure to preserve original video content, and limited support for fine-grained, iterative refinement. To address these challenges, we present PromptPoseFX, an interactive system that allows creators to author pose-driven visual effects through augmented language prompts and interactive refinement. Our system leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to translate high-level user intent into parameterized procedural graphics scripts, automatically mapping pose-tracking data to specific effect parameters, allowing precise alignment with human motion. This script-based approach manages effects as independent layers, thereby preserving the original content of the underlying video. To reduce language ambiguity, our interface offers controls across spatial, temporal, and parameter domains, enabling the precise, intuitive, and iterative authoring of pose-driven visual effects. We evaluated PromptPoseFX through a comparative study against a text-only LLM interface, followed by an exploratory study. In the comparative study, participants rated PromptPoseFX significantly higher than the text-only baseline on measures of perceived control and precision. The exploratory study examined usability and creativity support in open-ended authoring tasks.

papers.title: Vibe Interventions: Can Users Personalize and Iterate Their Way to Behavior Change?
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models allow a working application to be generated from natural-language description, and is referred to as generative user interfaces. Their application to behavior change is unexplored, and we provide one of the first controlled investigations of it. We distinguish two components of authorship: iteration, the revision of a generated artifact in natural language, and personalization, the conditioning of generation on stated context. In a pre-registered between-subjects experiment (N = 300, 60 per condition), we crossed these two factors and added a static intervention as a control, yielding five conditions; participants stated a goal and received a generated intervention. The personalized generative condition ranked highest on every self-report outcome, including ownership, satisfaction, and intended adoption. Randomized iteration had no detectable effect, and higher revision counts were negatively associated with evaluative ratings. This work establishes which component of authorship carries motivational value in generative behavior change tools.

papers.title: B2G-Agent: An LLM-Based Multi-Agent Tool for End-to-End Building-Grid Interactions
papers.abstract: Buildings are major electricity consumers and can interact with distribution network dispatch through flexible power scheduling. These interactions require distribution network operators (DNOs) and building energy managers (BEMs) to reconcile their operational constraints and perform complex cross-field computations. The lack of cross-domain expertise and unified computational workflows could lead to inefficient or physically infeasible interactions. To address this bottleneck, we develop an end-to-end large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent tool, B2G-Agent, that bridges DNOs and BEMs. The tool deploys three collaborative agents: a Translator for bidirectional cross-domain semantic mapping via hybrid retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); an Actor for automated configuration and execution of joint simulation and optimization through directed acyclic graphs; and a Reviewer for memory-augmented reflective failure diagnosis. This workflow abstracts away cross-field modeling complexities and enables both sides to focus on high-level operational decisions. Comprehensive evaluations across 200 synthesized tasks show that B2G-Agent improves the interaction quality score from 66.71 to 85.57 and increases the task success rate from 38.0% to 69.0% over the baseline while satisfying operational constraints. The open-source tool and interface are available at https://github.com/hkuedl/B2G-Agent.

papers.title: LLM Facilitation of Group Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Human groups often fail to integrate information distributed across their members, converging on incorrect decisions. We ask whether large language models (LLMs) can help groups reach the correct decision in such settings. In an online, chat-based experiment, 138 three-person groups (N = 414) completed a hidden-profile hiring task that required selecting the best candidate using public information available to all group members and private information available only to individual members. The randomized human-subject experiment included three conditions: no facilitation, an individual-level LLM that messaged each member privately, and a group-level LLM that messaged the whole group. The LLM facilitation consisted of adaptive interventions that summarized the discussion, nudged quiet members, and played devil's advocate. The LLM did not know which candidate was correct. Both LLM conditions significantly increased the rate at which groups reached consensus on the correct candidate, from 32.6% without facilitation to 56.5% with LLM facilitation. LLM-facilitated groups exchanged more consensus messages signaling agreement on the group's choice. Participants in the group-level condition also disclosed significantly more information about the correct candidate, whereas those receiving individual-level facilitation repeated public information less often. Finally, group-level facilitation received more favorable usability ratings than individual-level facilitation. These results show that LLMs can deliver adaptive, theory-informed interventions that improve group decision-making, and that the design of these interventions may shape how people respond to them.

papers.title: Personalization of Basic and Moral Values Guiding LLM-Controlled Assistant Robots
papers.abstract: Personal assistant robots powered by large language models (LLMs) are likely to enter everyday life within the next decade, but the values that should guide their behaviour remain largely unspecified. Current alignment practice steers a single model toward an aggregate of human values, ignoring that individual users may prefer a robot whose value profile differs from their own. We administer parallel self- and robot-targeted versions of three established psycho-metric instruments - the simplified Schwartz Values Survey (SVS), the Portrait Values Questionnaire (PVQ-21), and the Moral Foundations Questionnaire (MFQ) - to potential future users (N=22), capturing both their personal values and the values they would want an assistant robot to embody. We compare the three instruments as personalization tools using the UEQ-S and benchmark fifteen contemporary LLMs against the resulting profiles. Participants wanted their robot to score markedly lower than themselves on personal-focus values and higher on social-focus values; moral profiles were nearly identical. LLMs prompted to act as robots shifted only weakly toward the desired profile, indicating that default model behaviour and prompt engineering are no substitute for explicit value personalization.

papers.title: DECODE: Diagnosing Interpretability Failures in Automated Interpretation Process
papers.abstract: Tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on LLMs themselves to both generate and evaluate explanations, creating a self-referential automated interpretation process with minimal human oversight. This automation raises significant reliability concerns, which are exacerbated by the absence of ground truth. In practice, it is difficult to validate explanations or to attribute interpretability failures to their source -- whether they originate from the tool's extracted representations or from the LLM used in the process. To address these challenges, we present DECODE, a visual analytics system that reintroduces human oversight into the automated interpretation process. Our approach decomposes the diagnostic workflow into three progressive stages, isolating failure sources ranging from structural defects to explanation-level misalignments. Drawing inspiration from inter-coder consensus in qualitative analysis, we utilize consensus among independently generated explanations and their evaluation metrics as a proxy for reliability. To further scale human inspection, we employ a three-phase active seeding protocol that strategically recommends high-priority instances for manual review. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a case study on 16,384 Sparse Autoencoder features, showing that it can efficiently identify and attribute interpretability failures at scale.

papers.title: How Well Do Benchmarks Evaluate LLMs' Use for Personal Health Informatics?
papers.abstract: Benchmarking is a valuable technique for advancing the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), including in personal health informatics. There are growing efforts on benchmark creation for personal health data activities. However, it is unclear whether and how well these efforts align with needs and considerations of personal health informatics process. Addressing this need, we first analyzed 53,587 tasks across eight benchmarks related to personal health informatics and characterized the space of benchmark design. We then contrasted our observations of design choices with personal informatics theories and empirical knowledge. We find significant mismatches between existing benchmark design and domain guidelines and understanding. This lack of alignment limits the utility of the evidence current benchmarks offer about LLM capabilities. We use domain knowledge to highlight capabilities benchmarks should include and discuss opportunities our work enables for taking a human-centered and domain-driven approach to benchmark design.

papers.title: Multimodal Judges Flag, Humans Decide: A Review-and-Edit Framework for AI-Generated Product Video Ads
papers.abstract: Generative pipelines can now turn every product page of an e-commerce catalog into a short video ad, but deciding whether such an ad is usable is not one good-or-bad call. We describe how we operationalized the review and editing of these ads so that both can keep pace with generation: reviewers go through each ad scene by scene and answer six questions, on the product, scene quality, pronunciation, script, sound and captions; judges built from vision-language, speech and language models file each finding under the matching question, and reviewers accept or reject each finding and add what the judges missed. Each confirmed issue then opens an edit tool matched to it. The questions and the routing from a finding to its fix do not depend on the models that generate the ad. Across 120 ads from our pipeline, reviewed with judge findings on screen, reviewers marked the product wrong on 60% of scenes, and script, caption or sound problems on under 10% each. On 60 of these ads, they marked the product wrong on 58% of scenes, far more than the 26% marked by two reviewers who later saw the ads with the judges hidden; one reviewer who saw the ads both ways marked 57% with judge findings and 19% without. On 120 blind-labeled scenes, a product judge that watches the clip with the catalog photos reached AUC 0.84, while video-quality and photo-similarity scores were close to chance. We tune the judges for recall: the product judge catches nearly all defects but also flags many clean scenes, so reviewers decide; together, the judges widen what reviewers mark and reviewers add what the judges miss. Without judge findings, one reviewer's marking faded over a session. We release a review-portal template and our review data (120 ads and 562 scenes with judge findings and human marks, plus 120 blind-labeled scenes with baseline scores) at https://github.com/anoubhav/ad-review-and-edit.

papers.title: Code-Grounded Agentic Explanations for Static Analysis Vulnerability Findings
papers.abstract: Static application security testing (SAST) tools surface vulnerabilities early and their verdicts are rule-based and auditable. Yet developers routinely dismiss findings they cannot interpret. Large language models can supply the missing explanation, but designs that also hand the model the detection give up the auditability that makes static analysis defensible. We keep detection with the analyser and give the model only the explaining. A preliminary user study with 20 participants and a workshop with 19 practitioners yielded five requirements. Guided by these we redesigned SAFE, an open-source IntelliJ IDEA plugin that explains findings from any analyser reporting in the Static Analysis Results Interchange Format. It tiers explanations by demand, ties them to the reported data flow, and replaces the single-prompt backend with an agent that must consult the repository and the rule that fired before answering. A within-subjects crossover experiment with 24 participants compared the redesign against its predecessor. Perceived usability rose from 77.3 to 85.0 on the System Usability Scale. Actionability gained most among the explanation-quality items, the aspect both earlier studies flagged as weakest, and the odds of a correct remediation were 2.6 times higher. Triage accuracy and time per finding were indistinguishable, which we read as uninformative rather than as equivalence. Trust was the one measure that did not move, and the closing interviews indicate that grounding made findings easier to understand rather than easier to believe. Participants also drew a boundary no requirement anticipated, wanting the tool to find and explain while they judge and apply.
